description: Comprehensive question bank derived from the Minerals study material. Covers meaning, classification, physical properties, metallic/non-metallic/ferrous/non-ferrous/precious/industrial minerals, formation, distribution, uses, conservation, and Indian/Karnataka mineral geography. Verify and expand before formal examination use.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a mineral?

options.A: A naturally occurring, generally inorganic solid with a characteristic chemical composition and an ordered internal atomic structure
options.B: Any liquid or gas found underground
options.C: A rock composed of a single element only
options.D: Any substance mined from the earth, including petroleum

questions.explanation: A mineral is defined as a naturally occurring, generally inorganic solid with a characteristic chemical composition (or limited compositional range) and an ordered internal atomic structure.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an essential characteristic of a mineral?
questions.explanation: Minerals are generally inorganic in origin; organic origin is not an essential characteristic. The essential characteristics are natural occurrence, solid state, generally inorganic origin, characteristic chemical composition and ordered crystalline structure.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Are petroleum and natural gas minerals in the strict mineralogical sense?

options.A: Yes, because they are naturally occurring
options.B: No, they are not minerals in the strict mineralogical sense
options.C: Yes, because they have a characteristic chemical composition
options.D: Yes, because they have an ordered crystalline structure

questions.explanation: Petroleum and natural gas are not minerals in the strict mineralogical sense, even though they are naturally occurring substances.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Under what condition is natural ice recognised as a mineral?

options.B: When it occurs naturally as a solid
options.C: When it is mixed with salt
options.D: When it is found only in glaciers

questions.explanation: Natural ice is recognised as a mineral when it occurs naturally as a solid.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is mineralogy?

options.A: The study of rocks and their formation
options.B: The branch of geology that studies minerals, including composition, crystal structure, physical properties, origin and occurrence
options.D: The study of the earth's atmosphere

questions.explanation: Mineralogy is the branch of geology that studies minerals, including their composition, crystal structure, physical properties, origin and occurrence.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is an ore?

options.A: Any mineral found in the earth's crust
options.B: A naturally occurring material from which a useful metal or mineral can be extracted economically under prevailing conditions
options.C: A rock with no economic value

questions.explanation: An ore is a naturally occurring material from which a useful metal or mineral can be extracted economically under prevailing technological and market conditions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Are all minerals ores?

options.B: No, only mineral deposits that can be extracted economically for a useful component are ores
options.C: Yes, because all minerals contain metals
options.D: No, because ores are always organic

questions.explanation: Not all minerals are ores. Only mineral deposits that can be extracted economically for a useful component are ores. Economic viability changes with technology, prices and extraction costs.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is gangue?

options.A: The valuable metal in an ore
options.B: Unwanted or commercially less valuable minerals associated with an ore deposit
options.D: The process of extracting metal from ore

questions.explanation: Gangue refers to unwanted or commercially less valuable minerals associated with an ore deposit.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does a mineral differ from a rock?

options.A: A mineral is always larger than a rock
options.B: A mineral has a characteristic composition and crystal structure; a rock is an aggregate of one or more minerals or other geological materials
options.C: A rock has a characteristic composition; a mineral is an aggregate
options.D: There is no difference between a mineral and a rock

questions.explanation: A mineral has a characteristic composition and crystal structure; a rock is an aggregate of one or more minerals or other geological materials.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Granite is an example of which of the following?

options.C: A rock containing quartz, feldspar and mica

questions.explanation: Granite is a rock that contains quartz, feldspar and mica.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How are minerals commonly classified in economic geography?

options.A: Into metallic, non-metallic, ferrous, non-ferrous, precious and industrial minerals

questions.explanation: In economic geography, minerals are commonly classified into metallic, non-metallic, ferrous, non-ferrous, precious and industrial minerals.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following are major chemical classes of minerals?

options.A: Silicates, carbonates, oxides, sulphides, sulphates, halides, phosphates and native elements

questions.explanation: The major chemical classes of minerals are silicates, carbonates, oxides, sulphides, sulphates, halides, phosphates and native elements.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which minerals contain silicon and oxygen?
questions.explanation: Silicates contain silicon and oxygen. Examples include quartz, feldspar, mica and olivine.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a silicate mineral?
questions.explanation: Quartz is a silicate mineral containing silicon and oxygen. Calcite is a carbonate, galena a sulphide, and gypsum a sulphate.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which minerals contain the carbonate ion?
questions.explanation: Carbonates contain the carbonate ion. Examples include calcite and dolomite.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a carbonate mineral?
questions.explanation: Calcite is a carbonate mineral. Quartz is a silicate, hematite an oxide, and galena a sulphide.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which minerals contain oxygen combined with metals?
questions.explanation: Oxides contain oxygen combined with metals. Examples include hematite, magnetite and corundum.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an oxide mineral?
questions.explanation: Hematite is an oxide mineral. Calcite is a carbonate, gypsum a sulphate, and galena a sulphide.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which minerals contain sulphur with metals?
questions.explanation: Sulphides contain sulphur with metals. Examples include galena, sphalerite and chalcopyrite.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a sulphide mineral?
questions.explanation: Galena is a sulphide mineral. Quartz is a silicate, calcite a carbonate, and gypsum a sulphate.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which minerals contain the sulphate ion?
questions.explanation: Sulphates contain the sulphate ion. Examples include gypsum and barite.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a sulphate mineral?
questions.explanation: Gypsum is a sulphate mineral. Galena is a sulphide, hematite an oxide, and quartz a silicate.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following are halide minerals?
questions.explanation: Halides include halite (rock salt) and fluorite.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Apatite is an important mineral of which chemical class?
questions.explanation: Apatite is an important phosphate mineral.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following are native element minerals?

options.A: Gold, silver, copper, sulphur, graphite and diamond

questions.explanation: Native elements occur as elements; examples include gold, silver, copper, sulphur, graphite and diamond.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why are physical properties of minerals important?

options.A: They help identify minerals in hand specimens
options.B: They determine the price of minerals only
options.C: They are not useful for identification
options.D: They are used only in laboratories

questions.explanation: Physical properties help identify minerals in hand specimens, although reliable identification usually requires several properties together and sometimes laboratory tests.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is colour as a physical property of minerals?

options.A: The colour of a mineral in powdered form
options.B: The visible appearance of a mineral, which can be misleading due to impurities and weathering
options.C: The way a mineral reflects light
options.D: The resistance of a mineral to scratching

questions.explanation: Colour is the visible appearance of a mineral. It can be misleading because impurities and weathering may alter colour.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is streak?

options.A: The colour of a mineral in powdered form, usually observed on an unglazed porcelain streak plate
options.B: The way a mineral reflects light
options.D: The tendency to break along smooth planes

questions.explanation: Streak is the colour of a mineral in powdered form, usually observed on an unglazed porcelain streak plate. It is often more consistent than surface colour.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is lustre?

options.A: The colour of a mineral in powdered form
options.B: The way a mineral reflects light
options.D: The ratio of density to water

questions.explanation: Lustre is the way a mineral reflects light. Types include metallic, vitreous (glassy), pearly, silky, resinous, greasy and dull/earthy.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a type of lustre?
questions.explanation: Conchoidal is a type of fracture, not lustre. Lustre types include metallic, vitreous, pearly, silky, resinous, greasy and dull/earthy.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is hardness in minerals?

options.A: Resistance to scratching, commonly compared using the Mohs relative hardness scale
options.B: The way a mineral reflects light
options.C: The colour of a mineral in powdered form
options.D: The tendency to break along smooth planes

questions.explanation: Hardness is resistance to scratching, commonly compared using the Mohs relative hardness scale.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Mohs scale?

options.A: A linear scale of absolute hardness
options.B: A relative scale from 1 to 10 that is not a linear scale of absolute hardness

questions.explanation: The Mohs scale is a relative scale from 1 to 10. It is not a linear scale of absolute hardness.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which mineral has a Mohs hardness of 1?
questions.explanation: Talc is the softest reference mineral with a Mohs hardness of 1.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which mineral has a Mohs hardness of 2 and can be scratched by a fingernail?
questions.explanation: Gypsum has a Mohs hardness of 2 and can be scratched by a fingernail.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which mineral has a Mohs hardness of 3?
questions.explanation: Calcite has a reference hardness of 3 on the Mohs scale.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which mineral has a Mohs hardness of 4?
questions.explanation: Fluorite has a reference hardness of 4 on the Mohs scale.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which mineral has a Mohs hardness of 5?
questions.explanation: Apatite has a reference hardness of 5 on the Mohs scale.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which mineral has a Mohs hardness of 6 and can scratch glass in common tests?
questions.explanation: Orthoclase feldspar has a Mohs hardness of 6 and can scratch glass in common tests.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which mineral has a Mohs hardness of 7 and scratches glass?
questions.explanation: Quartz has a Mohs hardness of 7 and scratches glass.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which mineral has a Mohs hardness of 8?
questions.explanation: Topaz has a reference hardness of 8 on the Mohs scale.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which mineral has a Mohs hardness of 9 and includes ruby and sapphire?
questions.explanation: Corundum has a Mohs hardness of 9 and includes ruby and sapphire.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which mineral has a Mohs hardness of 10 and is the hardest natural mineral?
questions.explanation: Diamond has a Mohs hardness of 10 and is the hardest natural mineral on the Mohs scale.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is cleavage in minerals?

options.A: The tendency of a mineral to break along smooth, flat planes of weakness in its crystal structure
options.B: The way a mineral breaks where it does not split along cleavage planes
options.C: The characteristic external shape of a mineral
options.D: The ratio of density to water

questions.explanation: Cleavage is the tendency of a mineral to break along smooth, flat planes of weakness in its crystal structure.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is fracture in minerals?

options.A: The tendency to break along smooth, flat planes
options.B: The way a mineral breaks where it does not split along cleavage planes
options.C: The characteristic external shape of a mineral
options.D: The colour of a mineral in powdered form

questions.explanation: Fracture is the way a mineral breaks where it does not split along cleavage planes. Quartz commonly shows conchoidal (shell-like) fracture.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which mineral commonly shows conchoidal (shell-like) fracture?
questions.explanation: Quartz commonly shows conchoidal (shell-like) fracture.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is crystal habit?

options.A: The characteristic external shape of a mineral, such as cubic, prismatic, tabular, fibrous or needle-like
options.B: The tendency to break along smooth planes
options.C: The colour of a mineral in powdered form
options.D: The ratio of density to water

questions.explanation: Crystal habit is the characteristic external shape of a mineral, such as cubic, prismatic, tabular, fibrous or needle-like.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is specific gravity?

options.A: The ratio of a mineral's density to the density of water at a specified reference temperature
options.C: The way a mineral reflects light
options.D: The tendency to break along smooth planes

questions.explanation: Specific gravity is the ratio of a mineral's density to the density of water at a specified reference temperature.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is transparency as a physical property of minerals?

options.A: The degree to which light passes through a mineral: transparent, translucent or opaque
options.B: The way a mineral reflects light
options.C: The colour of a mineral in powdered form

questions.explanation: Transparency is the degree to which light passes through a mineral: transparent, translucent or opaque.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is magnetism as a physical property of minerals?

options.A: A mineral's response to a magnetic field; magnetite is strongly magnetic
options.B: The way a mineral reflects light
options.C: The tendency to break along smooth planes
options.D: The ratio of density to water

questions.explanation: Magnetism is a mineral's response to a magnetic field. Magnetite is strongly magnetic.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which mineral is strongly magnetic?
questions.explanation: Magnetite is strongly magnetic.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is tenacity in minerals?

options.A: How a mineral responds to bending, cutting, crushing or hammering; terms include brittle, malleable, ductile and flexible
options.B: The way a mineral reflects light
options.C: The colour of a mineral in powdered form
options.D: The tendency to break along smooth planes

questions.explanation: Tenacity is how a mineral responds to bending, cutting, crushing or hammering; terms include brittle, malleable, ductile and flexible.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does calcite react with dilute hydrochloric acid?

options.B: It effervesces because acid reacts with calcium carbonate and releases carbon dioxide

questions.explanation: Calcite effervesces with dilute hydrochloric acid because acid reacts with calcium carbonate and releases carbon dioxide.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does dolomite commonly react with dilute hydrochloric acid?

options.A: It reacts more vigorously than calcite
options.B: It reacts more slowly unless powdered
options.C: It does not react at all

questions.explanation: Dolomite commonly reacts more slowly than calcite unless powdered.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are metallic minerals?

options.A: Minerals mined chiefly because they contain or yield metals

questions.explanation: Metallic minerals are minerals mined chiefly because they contain or yield metals. Many have metallic or submetallic lustre, but this is not universal.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a metallic mineral?
questions.explanation: Hematite is an iron ore and a metallic mineral. Mica, gypsum and quartz are non-metallic minerals.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Chalcopyrite is an ore of which metal?
questions.explanation: Chalcopyrite is a major copper ore.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Bauxite is an ore of which metal?
questions.explanation: Bauxite is the principal ore of aluminium.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Galena is an ore of which metal?
questions.explanation: Galena is a major lead ore.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Sphalerite is an ore of which metal?
questions.explanation: Sphalerite is a major zinc ore.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Cassiterite is the principal ore of which metal?
questions.explanation: Cassiterite is the principal tin ore.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the main uses of metallic minerals?

options.A: They supply metals for construction, transport, machinery, electrical equipment, electronics, packaging, tools and manufacturing
options.B: They are used only as fertilisers
options.C: They are used only in jewellery
options.D: They are used only for glassmaking

questions.explanation: Metallic minerals supply metals for construction, transport, machinery, electrical equipment, electronics, packaging, tools and manufacturing.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are non-metallic minerals?

options.A: Minerals not mined primarily to extract metals; used directly or processed for industrial, construction, agricultural and chemical purposes
options.B: Minerals that contain no useful elements

questions.explanation: Non-metallic minerals are minerals not mined primarily to extract metals; they are used directly or processed for industrial, construction, agricultural and chemical purposes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is a non-metallic mineral?
questions.explanation: Mica is a non-metallic mineral. Hematite, chalcopyrite and galena are metallic minerals.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is a non-metallic mineral used in electrical insulation?
questions.explanation: Mica is a non-metallic mineral used in electrical insulation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the uses of non-metallic minerals?

options.A: Cement, ceramics, glass, fertilisers, chemicals, paints, paper, electrical insulation, cosmetics, construction and agriculture

questions.explanation: Non-metallic minerals are used in cement, ceramics, glass, fertilisers, chemicals, paints, paper, electrical insulation, cosmetics, construction and agriculture.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Is bauxite non-metallic because it looks earthy?

options.A: Yes, because it is earthy in appearance
options.B: No, bauxite is the principal aluminium ore and is classified as a metallic mineral resource in economic geography
options.C: Yes, because it contains no metal
options.D: Yes, because it is used only in cement

questions.explanation: Bauxite is the principal aluminium ore and is classified as a metallic mineral resource in economic geography, despite its earthy appearance.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are ferrous minerals in economic geography?
questions.explanation: Ferrous minerals in economic geography are iron-associated metallic mineral resources. School-level classifications commonly include iron ore, manganese and chromite because of their importance to the iron and steel industry.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following are commonly included as ferrous minerals in school-level classification?
questions.explanation: School-level classifications commonly include iron ore, manganese and chromite as ferrous minerals because of their importance to the iron and steel industry.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the main iron ores?
questions.explanation: The main iron ores are hematite and magnetite; limonite and siderite are also iron-bearing ores.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is an important iron ore that is strongly magnetic?
questions.explanation: Magnetite is an iron oxide mineral, strongly magnetic and an important iron ore.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is hematite?

options.A: An iron oxide mineral, an important iron ore, commonly reddish-brown to steel-grey

questions.explanation: Hematite is an iron oxide mineral, an important iron ore, commonly reddish-brown to steel-grey.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why is manganese important?

options.A: It is used in steelmaking as a deoxidising and alloying element, and in batteries and chemicals
options.B: It is used only in jewellery
options.C: It is used only in glassmaking
options.D: It is used only as a fertiliser

questions.explanation: Manganese is used in steelmaking as a deoxidising and alloying element, and in batteries and chemicals.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why is chromite important?

options.A: It is the principal ore of chromium, used in stainless steel, alloy steels, plating and refractory materials
options.B: It is the principal ore of aluminium
options.C: It is the principal ore of copper
options.D: It is the principal ore of gold

questions.explanation: Chromite is the principal ore of chromium, used in stainless steel, alloy steels, plating and refractory materials.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are non-ferrous minerals?

options.A: Metallic mineral resources yielding metals other than iron or not primarily classified as iron-based

questions.explanation: Non-ferrous minerals are metallic mineral resources yielding metals other than iron or not primarily classified as iron-based.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a non-ferrous mineral?
questions.explanation: Bauxite (aluminium) is a non-ferrous mineral. Hematite and magnetite are iron ores, and chromite is commonly grouped with ferrous minerals in school classification.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the uses of copper?

options.A: Electrical wiring, motors, electronics, plumbing and alloys because of high electrical and thermal conductivity

questions.explanation: Copper is used in electrical wiring, motors, electronics, plumbing and alloys because of high electrical and thermal conductivity.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the uses of aluminium?

options.A: Aircraft, transport, packaging, construction, electrical transmission and household products because it is lightweight and corrosion-resistant

questions.explanation: Aluminium is used in aircraft, transport, packaging, construction, electrical transmission and household products because it is lightweight and corrosion-resistant.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the uses of lead?
questions.explanation: Lead is used in lead-acid batteries and radiation shielding.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the main uses of zinc?

options.A: Galvanising steel, brass, die-casting and chemicals

questions.explanation: Zinc is used mainly for galvanising steel, brass, die-casting and chemicals.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How do ferrous and non-ferrous metals differ?

options.A: Ferrous metals are iron-based; non-ferrous metals are not primarily iron-based
options.B: Ferrous metals are magnetic; non-ferrous metals are not magnetic
options.C: Ferrous metals are precious; non-ferrous metals are not
options.D: Ferrous metals are non-metallic; non-ferrous metals are metallic

questions.explanation: Ferrous metals are iron-based; non-ferrous metals are not primarily iron-based. The distinction is not simply whether a mineral is magnetic.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are precious minerals in economic geography?

options.A: High-value metals and gemstones used in jewellery, investment and specialised applications

questions.explanation: In economic geography, precious minerals commonly cover high-value metals and gemstones used in jewellery, investment and specialised applications.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following are precious metals?
questions.explanation: Gold, silver and platinum are precious metals.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following are gemstones?
questions.explanation: Diamond, ruby, sapphire and emerald are gemstones.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is diamond?

options.A: A crystalline form of native carbon and the hardest natural mineral on the Mohs scale; used in jewellery and industrial cutting, drilling and abrasives

questions.explanation: Diamond is a crystalline form of native carbon and the hardest natural mineral on the Mohs scale; it is used in jewellery and industrial cutting, drilling and abrasives.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Ruby and sapphire are gem varieties of which mineral?
questions.explanation: Ruby and sapphire are gem varieties of corundum. Ruby is typically red; sapphire occurs in several colours, commonly blue.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is emerald?

options.A: A green gem variety of beryl, with colour commonly associated with chromium and/or vanadium
options.B: A red gem variety of corundum
options.C: A blue gem variety of corundum

questions.explanation: Emerald is a green gem variety of beryl, with colour commonly associated with chromium and/or vanadium.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why are gold and silver valuable?

options.A: They are relatively scarce, workable and corrosion-resistant metals used in jewellery, investment, electronics and other industries
options.D: They are used only as fertilisers

questions.explanation: Gold and silver are valuable because they are relatively scarce, workable and corrosion-resistant metals used in jewellery, investment, electronics and other industries.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are industrial minerals?

options.A: Non-fuel mineral materials used for their physical or chemical properties in manufacturing, construction, agriculture and other industries, rather than chiefly as metal ores

questions.explanation: Industrial minerals are non-fuel mineral materials used for their physical or chemical properties in manufacturing, construction, agriculture and other industries, rather than chiefly as metal ores.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which minerals are used in cement?
questions.explanation: Limestone and gypsum are used in cement. Limestone supplies calcium; clay or shale supplies silica and alumina; gypsum regulates setting.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which mineral is used in glassmaking?
questions.explanation: Silica sand is the main raw material in glassmaking; soda ash and limestone are also commonly used.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which mineral is used in electrical insulation?
questions.explanation: Mica is used in electrical insulation.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which mineral is used in ceramics and paper?
questions.explanation: Kaolin is used in ceramics and paper.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which mineral is used in fertilisers?
questions.explanation: Phosphorite is used in fertilisers. Phosphate minerals such as apatite/phosphorite supply phosphorus; potash minerals supply potassium.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why is silica important?

options.A: Silica, commonly obtained from quartz or silica sand, is used in glassmaking, foundry work, construction materials and silicon-related industries
options.B: Silica is used only as a fertiliser
options.C: Silica is the principal ore of aluminium

questions.explanation: Silica, commonly obtained from quartz or silica sand, is used in glassmaking, foundry work, construction materials and silicon-related industries.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is used in paints, paper and ceramics?
questions.explanation: Talc is used in paints, paper and ceramics.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which mineral is used in chemical and metallurgical uses?
questions.explanation: Fluorite is used in chemical and metallurgical uses.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How are minerals formed?

options.A: Through crystallisation from magma or lava, precipitation from water, deposition from hydrothermal fluids, metamorphic reactions, evaporation and biological activity

questions.explanation: Minerals are formed through crystallisation from magma or lava, precipitation from water, deposition from hydrothermal fluids, metamorphic reactions, evaporation and biological activity.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How do minerals form from magma?

options.A: As magma cools, elements combine and crystallise at different temperatures, forming minerals such as olivine, pyroxene, amphibolite, feldspar and quartz
options.B: Through evaporation of saline water only

questions.explanation: As magma cools, elements combine and crystallise at different temperatures, forming minerals such as olivine, pyroxene, amphibolite, feldspar and quartz.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How do hydrothermal minerals form?

options.A: Hot mineral-rich fluids circulate through fractures and pores; changes in temperature, pressure or chemistry cause dissolved substances to precipitate as veins or replacement deposits
options.B: Through evaporation of saline water only

questions.explanation: Hot mineral-rich fluids circulate through fractures and pores. Changes in temperature, pressure or chemistry cause dissolved substances to precipitate as veins or replacement deposits.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How do sedimentary minerals form?

options.A: By chemical precipitation from water, evaporation of saline water, or accumulation and alteration of sediments and biological material

questions.explanation: Sedimentary minerals form by chemical precipitation from water, evaporation of saline water, or accumulation and alteration of sediments and biological material.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How do metamorphic minerals form?

options.A: Existing minerals react and recrystallise under changed temperature, pressure and fluid conditions, producing minerals stable under the new conditions

questions.explanation: Metamorphic minerals form when existing minerals react and recrystallise under changed temperature, pressure and fluid conditions, producing minerals stable under the new conditions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are placer deposits?

options.A: Concentrations of resistant, dense minerals produced when water or waves sort sediments by density
options.B: Deposits left when weathering removes soluble components

questions.explanation: Placer deposits are concentrations of resistant, dense minerals produced when water or waves sort sediments by density. Gold, cassiterite and some gemstones can form placer deposits.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following can form placer deposits?
questions.explanation: Gold, cassiterite and some gemstones can form placer deposits.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are residual deposits?

options.A: Deposits left when weathering removes soluble or less resistant components and concentrates relatively insoluble material; lateritic bauxite is an example
options.D: Deposits formed by evaporation of saline water

questions.explanation: Residual deposits are deposits left when weathering removes soluble or less resistant components and concentrates relatively insoluble material. Lateritic bauxite is an example.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Are minerals evenly distributed across Earth?

options.B: No, their distribution is highly uneven because deposits depend on geological history, rock type, tectonic setting, climate, weathering and sedimentary processes
options.C: Yes, because all rocks contain all minerals
options.D: No, because minerals are only found in deserts

questions.explanation: Minerals are not evenly distributed across Earth. Their distribution is highly uneven because deposits depend on geological history, rock type, tectonic setting, climate, weathering and sedimentary processes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following statements about minerals is correct?

options.A: A mineral has a characteristic chemical composition and an ordered internal atomic structure
options.B: All naturally occurring substances are minerals
options.C: Petroleum is a mineral in the strict mineralogical sense
options.D: A rock is a single mineral

questions.explanation: A mineral has a characteristic chemical composition (or limited compositional range) and an ordered internal atomic structure. Not all naturally occurring substances are minerals; petroleum and natural gas are not minerals in the strict mineralogical sense; a rock is an aggregate of one or more minerals or other geological materials.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following statements about ores is correct?

options.A: Only mineral deposits that can be extracted economically for a useful component are ores
options.D: Economic viability of an ore never changes

questions.explanation: Only mineral deposits that can be extracted economically for a useful component are ores. Economic viability changes with technology, prices and extraction costs.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following statements about mineral classification is correct?

options.A: In economic geography, minerals are classified into metallic, non-metallic, ferrous, non-ferrous, precious and industrial minerals; mineralogists also classify them by chemical composition
options.B: Minerals are classified only by colour
options.C: Minerals are classified only by hardness
options.D: Minerals are classified only into metallic and non-metallic

questions.explanation: In economic geography, minerals are commonly classified into metallic, non-metallic, ferrous, non-ferrous, precious and industrial minerals. Mineralogists also classify them by chemical composition.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the Mohs scale is correct?

options.A: It is a relative scale from 1 to 10 and is not a linear scale of absolute hardness
options.B: It is a linear scale of absolute hardness

questions.explanation: The Mohs scale is a relative scale from 1 to 10. It is not a linear scale of absolute hardness.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following statements about streak and colour is correct?

options.A: Streak is often more consistent than surface colour because colour can be misleading due to impurities and weathering
options.B: Surface colour is always more reliable than streak
options.C: Streak and surface colour are always identical
options.D: Streak is the way a mineral reflects light

questions.explanation: Colour can be misleading because impurities and weathering may alter colour. Streak, the colour of a mineral in powdered form, is often more consistent than surface colour.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following statements about ferrous minerals is correct?

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the ferrous/non-ferrous distinction is correct?

options.A: Ferrous means iron-based; non-ferrous means not primarily iron-based; the distinction is not simply whether a mineral is magnetic
options.B: Ferrous means magnetic; non-ferrous means non-magnetic
options.C: Ferrous means precious; non-ferrous means non-precious
options.D: Ferrous means metallic; non-ferrous means non-metallic

questions.explanation: Ferrous metals are iron-based; non-ferrous metals are not primarily iron-based. The distinction is not simply whether a mineral is magnetic.

questions.explanation: Industrial minerals are non-fuel mineral materials used for their physical or chemical properties in manufacturing, construction, agriculture and other industries, rather than chiefly as metal ores.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following statements about mineral formation is correct?

options.A: Minerals form through crystallisation from magma or lava, precipitation from water, deposition from hydrothermal fluids, metamorphic reactions, evaporation and biological activity
options.B: Minerals form only through volcanic eruptions
options.D: Minerals form only through biological activity

questions.explanation: Minerals are formed through crystallisation from magma or lava, precipitation from water, deposition from hydrothermal fluids, metamorphic reactions, evaporation and biological activity.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following statements about placer and residual deposits is correct?

options.A: Placer deposits are concentrations of resistant, dense minerals produced when water or waves sort sediments by density; residual deposits are left when weathering removes soluble or less resistant components and concentrates relatively insoluble material
options.B: Placer deposits are formed by magma cooling; residual deposits are formed by hydrothermal fluids
options.C: Placer deposits are formed by evaporation; residual deposits are formed by metamorphism
options.D: Placer and residual deposits are the same thing

questions.explanation: Placer deposits are concentrations of resistant, dense minerals produced when water or waves sort sediments by density. Residual deposits are left when weathering removes soluble or less resistant components and concentrates relatively insoluble material. Lateritic bauxite is an example of a residual deposit.

options.D: Mineral distribution is controlled only by climate

questions.subject: Geography

options.C: A resource is a type of rock; a reserve is a type of mineral
options.D: There is no difference between a resource and a reserve

questions.explanation: A resource is a concentration with reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction; a reserve is the economically mineable part after technical, economic and other modifying factors are considered.

questions.explanation: Recycling recovers metals from scrap and discarded products, reducing demand for new mining, energy and waste. Benefits vary by material and process.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following statements about beneficiation and mine reclamation is correct?

options.A: Beneficiation is processing mined ore to improve its grade or value by separating valuable minerals from gangue; mine reclamation is restoring mined land to a stable and useful condition
options.B: Beneficiation is restoring mined land; mine reclamation is separating gangue
options.C: Beneficiation and mine reclamation are the same thing
options.D: Beneficiation is recycling metals; mine reclamation is mining ore

questions.explanation: Beneficiation is processing mined ore to improve its grade or value by separating valuable minerals from gangue. Mine reclamation is restoring mined land to a stable and useful condition, including reshaping land, replacing soil, controlling pollution and re-establishing vegetation.
